newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: WHEAT--Argentine sales said nearing 3 mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT--Argentine sales said nearing 3 mln tonnes.

text.p: Export sales of Argentina's bumper 1996/97 wheat harvest are nearing three million tonnes, leaving six million to seven million tonnes still to place, traders said Monday.
Traders agreed the vast bulk of the crop is still to be priced, leaving plenty of room for millions more tonnes of Argentine wheat at possibly even lower prices.

"The farmers here are a bunch of losers. They have an array of futures and financial instruments at their disposal, and they don't use them. So what if they don't like the price now, they've got no choice," said one trader.
Argentine wheat was offered at $128 a tonne FOB for January to March shipment Monday, down by about $10 in the past week and down by about $100 since May.

One trader said that he thought export sales totalled 3.0 million tonnes, while exporters had bought around 2.2 million tonnes from local farmers. Another trader thought sales might have made it as high as 3.2 million tonnes.

But a third put sales at just 2.5-2.8 million tonnes. He said that some optional sales which had previously been computed as Argentine had ended up going to wheat from other origins. In one case, Australian wheat had replaced Argentine grain in a sale to Jordan, he said.

Due to a combination of higher sown area, more fertilization and better luck with weather, Argentina's wheat harvest is seen rising to as much as 15 million tonnes, up from just over nine million tonnes in drought-blighted 1995/96. U.S. consultants Sparks Cos said last week it thought Argentine wheat exports would almost double to 9.6 million tonnes.

The main pressure of the harvest is still to hit the market, with the crops just beginning to be gathered in the most northernly stretches of the wheat belt, and some feared that the price differential with foreign wheat could widen.
"I think the spread with other origins is going to broaden by $10 during the harvest," a trader said, adding that Argentine wheat was now about $20 cheaper than French wheat.
But other traders were unsure if the harvest will push prices down so much, and pointed out that big improvements in port and loading facilities should help stave off bottlenecks.
"Maybe December will be a bit hectic, with 1.5 million tonnes due for shipping, mainly from river ports. But January and February should go fairly smoothly," one trader said.

Farmers may also be in a better financial position to fund their harvesting, without having to resort to making big spot sales. Only a small proportion of the crop was pre-sold on futures markets, but the good prices at which it was placed means many farmers have more money in the bank than usual.
But traders agreed that the big determinant of prices will be the international market.

"Think that Canada, with 20 million tonnes to export, has only exported 4.5 million tonnes. Australia, with 15 million tonnes to export, has not exported much. So prices could fall with so much wheat left to hit the market," one said.

Another factor is whether the European Union further boosts its subsidies, provoking possible responses from the United States and Canada. One of the reasons Europe has ratched up its subsidies is cheap Argentine wheat, some of which has been competing with European wheat in some markets.
But one trader snorted "The Europeans don't have any natural markets. They can only sell anywhere because of their subsidies."
